O.outcome_detail: Potential false positives and false negatives in identifying potential English learners

cells.quote: Home language surveys are usually administered to the adults enrolling a child as part of initial registration with the school district. Depending upon the number and nature of questions asked, surveys can “cast their net” widely or narrowly in defining the pool of students for further assessment. This has implications for the resources states must expend at this and subsequent stages. It also affects the potential for generating “false positives” (students wrongly identified as potential EL when they are in fact not), as well as “false negatives” (students not properly identified as EL because they are omitted from initial assessment).
cells.note: The study presents a narrative discussion of variation and implications, not a quantified treatment-comparison finding; it does not specify whether widely or narrowly cast surveys produce more false positives or false negatives.

O.outcome_detail: factor structure, variance explained, and item loadings

cells.quote: A second EFA was conducted on the remaining 39 items. The KMO value was 0.958, and Bartlett’s test was significant (χ2 = 17129.998, p < 0.01). Six factors with eigenvalues > 1 were extracted, explaining 72.558% of the variance, and all 39 items had factor loadings exceeding 0.50 (range: 0.511–0.855) (see Table 2).

O.outcome_detail: confirmatory factor-model fit

cells.quote: CFA was conducted on the validation sample (n = 393) to test the six-factor structure of the 39-item HLC-N. As shown in Table 3, the model demonstrated good fit: χ2/df = 2.223 (< 3.0), RMSEA = 0.056 (< 0.08), CFI = 0.942, NFI = 0.900, IFI = 0.942, TLI = 0.937 (all > 0.90), and GFI = 0.830 (> 0.80).
cells.note: The study tested psychometric model fit rather than comparing instructional treatments; the contrast is represented against the study's stated recommended fit thresholds.
